The New Testament places the latter days in the present (Acts 2:17; 1 Corinthians 10:11). The picture is of nations being taught and changed, not destroyed, which suits gradual conversion; judgment and peace come through instruction going out from Zion, which matches the Great Commission going out from Jerusalem (Luke 24:47).
Critics say the world has not seen a general end to war in the two millennia since, and amillennialists say the perfect peace described points to the new creation rather than to a stage in history.

The prophecy is fulfilled in the church (spiritual Zion) as people from all nations come to Christ now, and is consummated in the new heavens and new earth, where war is no more. It does not describe an intermediate millennial age with a rebuilt Jerusalem.
Hebrews 12:22 identifies Zion with the heavenly city that believers have already come to, and Revelation 21-22 pictures the nations walking in the light of the city in the new creation.

Premillennialists say the oracle describes a period in which nations still need judging and arbitration (2:4), which does not fit the eternal state. Postmillennialists say amillennialism postpones its historical aspect too much.

The prophecy partly began with the gospel's spread, but its picture of universal peace among nations who still need arbitration (2:4) fits best the earthly reign of Christ after his return, before the eternal state.
The oracle includes nations being judged and taught, which implies a world where sin is still present but restrained. That is what premillennialists expect in the millennium.
Amillennialists answer that the prophets regularly describe the eternal state with imagery from their own world, so arbitration between nations need not imply continuing sin.

This is a literal prophecy of the millennial kingdom. Physical Mount Zion in Jerusalem will be elevated (compare Zechariah 14:10), the millennial temple will be there, and the nations will come to Jerusalem to be taught by the Messiah reigning on David's throne, while war ceases worldwide.

The oracle uses specific geographic terms (Zion, Jerusalem, the house of the God of Jacob), and the companion passage Micah 4 adds that each will sit under his vine and fig tree, which implies an earthly, agricultural setting.
Critics argue that the New Testament reinterprets Zion and the temple in terms of Christ and the church (John 2:19-21; Hebrews 12:22), so a physical temple centre would reverse that fulfilment.

The “latter days” are the last days of the old covenant age, from Christ to AD 70 (Hebrews 1:2; 9:26). After the earthly temple was removed, the true house of the LORD, Christ and his church, was established as the chief mountain, and from then on the nations stream into it.
The New Testament writers speak of living in the last days in their own time (Acts 2:16-17; 1 Peter 1:20), and the destruction of the old temple cleared the way for the new.
Critics argue that New Testament “last days” describe the whole period from Christ's first coming to his second, not only the forty years to AD 70.
The Increase of His Government

A child is born and a son given, on whose shoulder the government rests; he is called Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God (ʾel gibbor), Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. “Of the increase (marbeh) of his government and of peace there will be no end”, on the throne of David, established with justice and righteousness forever. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this.

When the child sits on David's throne and what “increase without end” means: continual growth of Christ's present reign through history, the eternal reign that begins at his return, or a literal Davidic throne in Jerusalem after the return. Matthew 4:15-16 applies Isaiah 9:1-2 to Jesus' Galilean ministry, and Luke 1:32-33 echoes 9:7.

The child is Jesus, who took up David's throne at his resurrection and ascension. His government will increase continually and without end, starting from small beginnings and growing through history, which is how postmillennialists read the progress of the gospel. The guarantee is the zeal of the LORD of hosts (9:7), not human effort.

Marbeh speaks of increase or growth, not mere duration, which matches the kingdom parables of growth (Matthew 13:31-33). The throne of David is linked to Christ's resurrection and enthronement (Acts 2:30-31).
Critics say that “no end” may describe the permanence of the kingdom rather than continuous growth in history, and that the history of the church shows decline as well as growth.

This prophecy is fulfilled in Christ's present reign on David's throne at the Father's right hand, which expands as the gospel goes to the nations and lasts eternally. There is no separate future Davidic reign in Jerusalem; the eternal kingdom begun at the first advent is consummated at the return.
The prophecy emphasises the eternal (“forever”), not a thousand-year reign, and the New Testament presents the risen Christ as already on David's throne (Acts 2:30-36; 13:34).
Premillennialists argue that the throne of David is a specific, earthly throne in Jerusalem, so heaven cannot be its location.

The child is Jesus, and his rule was inaugurated at his exaltation, but the full, visible reign of justice and peace on David's throne will appear when he returns to reign on earth, and it will continue without end into the eternal state.

The promise of justice and peace established on David's throne describes a visible order on earth, which premillennialists think the present age does not fulfil. Luke 1:32-33 promises Jesus a reign 'over the house of Jacob', which they expect to be openly realised when he returns.
Amillennialists answer that the eternal character of the reign does not fit a limited millennium, and postmillennialists that it fits the present reign.

The birth was fulfilled at the first advent, but the reign on David's throne is future: Christ will sit on David's literal throne in Jerusalem in the millennium and reign forever. Between the two lies the church age, which the prophet did not see. This is a classic case of prophetic “gap”.

Luke 1:32-33 promises Jesus the throne of his father David and a reign over the house of Jacob, which dispensationalists take as national and literal. Jesus did not reign over Israel in that sense at his first coming.
Critics argue that Peter in Acts 2:30-36 says Christ was raised and exalted precisely to sit on David's throne.
Christ's government was fully established in AD 70 when the old covenant age ended, and it now increases forever; there is no future consummation in which the kingdom changes.
Full preterists see the present eternal reign without end as the kingdom fully come, which fits the endless increase of 9:7.
Critics argue that the full justice and peace described is not present in the world, and that the view leaves no future for the bodily resurrection confessed in the creeds.
New Heavens and a New Earth

God announces that he creates new heavens and a new earth; Jerusalem will be a joy; weeping will not be heard. Yet the passage goes on to say that one who dies at a hundred will be considered young, and the sinner who reaches a hundred is accursed (65:20). People will build and plant and enjoy their work; the wolf and the lamb will feed together (65:25).

The passage calls itself “new heavens and a new earth” but still includes death, sinners and a long lifespan. Is this the eternal state described in the language of Isaiah's time (with long life as a picture of no death), a millennial kingdom with death still present, or the new covenant era (the gospel age), which partial preterists and postmillennialists call the “new creation” already begun?

This is the new creation already begun in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17), described in the gospel age as it reaches maturity. Because death and sin still exist, it cannot be the eternal state. It describes the long-term flourishing of Christ's kingdom in history, with prosperity, long life, peace and justice increasing as the gospel transforms society.
Death and sinners are present (65:20), which excludes the eternal state; but the passage also calls itself new creation, which fits the new covenant era inaugurated by Christ.

Amillennialists answer that Revelation 21:1-4, which takes up this prophecy, applies it to the eternal state with no death. Premillennialists answer that the passage describes conditions after a decisive divine intervention, not a gradual process.

This is the eternal state, but Isaiah describes it in the terms of his own time: a lifespan of a hundred years would be extraordinary to the original hearers, a way of saying death has lost its power. Revelation 21:1-4 confirms that the reference is to the consummated new creation, and the fulfilment begins with Christ's first advent.
Isaiah himself calls the scene new heavens and a new earth (65:17; 66:22), and Revelation 21 takes it up for the eternal state. Prophetic language naturally pictures the future in present-day images.
Premillennialists and postmillennialists argue that a sinner dying at a hundred cannot describe a world without sin and death; reading it as symbolic seems to evade the text.

The passage describes the millennial kingdom, in which life is long but death and sin are not yet removed, a stage before the eternal state that only premillennialism has a place for. Grudem lists Isaiah 65:20 among the main Old Testament supports for a future millennium.
The conditions (death, but at an advanced age; a curse on sinners; animals at peace) fit neither the present age nor the eternal state, which suggests an intermediate earthly kingdom.

Critics answer that the passage itself calls the period “new heavens and new earth”, which Revelation 21 uses for the eternal state, so splitting the passage between millennium and eternity is hard to justify.

Many dispensationalists (Walvoord, Pentecost) take 65:17-19 as looking to the eternal state and 65:20-25 as describing the millennial kingdom, centred on Jerusalem, with long life and restored nature. Others read the whole passage as millennial, with the eternal state as its final form.
The presence of death, building, planting and childbirth requires an earthly, pre-eternal kingdom in which Israel is restored in its land.

Critics argue that a shift from the eternal state to the millennium mid-passage has no textual marker, and that the passage is consistent if read either as a single picture of the consummation or as a picture of the present age.

The new heavens and new earth are the new covenant order that replaced the old covenant world (Hebrews 8:13). It was established in Christ and confirmed when the old order ended in AD 70. It then develops in history, which is why death and sin can still appear in it. A final consummation follows at Christ's return.
Old Testament “heavens and earth” language can describe a covenant order (Isaiah 51:15-16; Deuteronomy 32:1), and the new covenant is new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17; Galatians 6:15).
Critics argue that 2 Peter 3:10-13 and Revelation 21 describe a cosmic renewal and the removal of death, which has not yet occurred, so the covenantal reading at most captures part of the meaning.

The new heavens and new earth of Isaiah 65 and Revelation 21 are the new covenant world, fully arrived in AD 70. There is no future cosmic renewal; the passage describes the present spiritual reality of the church.
Full preterists argue that the passage itself shows that the new heavens and earth contain death and sin, which makes it the present age rather than a future perfect world.

Critics answer that Revelation 21:4 explicitly removes death, and that Romans 8:18-23 expects creation itself to be freed from corruption. They note that denying a future renewal departs from historic orthodoxy.
One Nation, One Shepherd, One Sanctuary

After the vision of the dry bones (37:1–14) and the sign of the two sticks (37:15–20), God promises to gather Israel from the nations into its own land, make Judah and Ephraim one nation under one king, 'my servant David', cleanse them from idolatry, make an everlasting covenant of peace, and set his sanctuary among them forever, so that the nations will know the LORD sanctifies Israel.

Is this a promise of a future national, territorial restoration of ethnic Israel under the Messiah, or is it fulfilled in Christ (the Davidic shepherd) and his one new-covenant people, as the New Testament's reuse of 37:27 in 2 Corinthians 6:16 and Revelation 21:3 suggests?

A literal promise to the physical descendants of Jacob: regathering to the land God gave Jacob (37:25), national reunification, and the reign of the Messiah, David's greater Son, from Jerusalem during the millennium. Many dispensationalists see the modern return to the land (1948 onward) as a preparatory, still-unbelieving stage (compare the bones assembling before breath enters, 37:7–10), with spiritual regeneration to follow at Christ's return.

The text is concrete and geographical ('the land I gave to my servant Jacob, where your fathers lived'), and the promise is called unconditional and everlasting (37:25–26). A consistent grammatical-historical reading, it is argued, should not transfer promises made to Israel to a different referent.

Critics reply that the New Testament itself applies the covenant formula of 37:27 to the mixed Jewish-Gentile church (2 Corinthians 6:16) and the 'one shepherd' theme to Jesus gathering 'other sheep' (John 10:16), indicating that the apostles read the passage as fulfilled in Christ. Dispensationalists answer that an application to the church does not exhaust the original promise to Israel.

The promise is fulfilled in Jesus, the true David and good shepherd, who gathers one flock from Israel and the nations; the 'sanctuary among them' is God's dwelling in Christ and the church as temple, consummated in the new creation where 'the dwelling of God is with man' (Revelation 21:3). Land promises expand to the renewed earth (Romans 4:13; Matthew 5:5).

The New Testament reuses this very passage for the church (2 Corinthians 6:16) and for the final state (Revelation 21:3); Jesus identifies himself as the one shepherd (John 10:11–16); Ephesians 2:14–22 describes the uniting of divided peoples into one temple.

Dispensationalists object that this is replacement theology that empties the 'David', 'land' and 'Judah and Ephraim' particulars of meaning. Amillennialists respond that fulfilment in Christ is not replacement but escalation: believing Israel is the root of the one people, and the promises are kept 'in a more glorious way'.

Agrees that the passage is fulfilled in Christ and his church, but many postmillennialists (following the Puritan hope) add that Romans 11 predicts a large-scale conversion of ethnic Jews within history, which will be a striking instance of the 'one flock' and help usher in a period of gospel blessing among the nations.
Romans 11:12, 15, 25–26 links Israel's 'fullness' to 'life from the dead' for the world; the Puritan and Princeton tradition read Ezekiel's restoration through that lens.

Amillennialists counter that 'all Israel' in Romans 11:26 may be the elect remnant across the age, not a future mass conversion; dispensationalists object that conversion without land restoration still spiritualizes 37:25.

Historic premillennialists are divided. Ladd held that the New Testament reinterprets Old Testament Israel promises in the church, while others in the tradition expect a future turning of ethnic Israel and see a partial earthly fulfilment in Christ's millennial reign before the eternal state brings the 'everlasting' aspects to completion.
The two-stage hope (millennium, then new creation) gives room for both an earthly reign of the Davidic king (Revelation 20) and an everlasting sanctuary (Revelation 21:3).
Dispensationalists think Ladd conceded too much; amillennialists think inserting a millennium adds a stage the passage does not require.

Jesus is the true Israel and Davidic king; the promise is fulfilled typologically in him and in all united to him, Jew and Gentile alike. The land functions as a type of the whole new creation, so the 'everlasting' land promise is kept in the renewed cosmos rather than in a territorial restoration in the present age.
Reads Ezekiel 37 along the canonical storyline of the covenants, in which Christ fulfils Israel's vocation and the new covenant forms one people (Ephesians 2:11–22; Hebrews 8).
Dispensational critics say typology is used to override the plain sense of the text; covenant theologians say the view underplays continuity with the believing Israel of old.
Ezekiel's Temple Vision and the River of Life

In 573 BC Ezekiel is taken in visions to a very high mountain and shown, by a man with a measuring line, a vast temple complex (chs. 40–43), the return of God's glory, regulations for priests, a prince, offerings and festivals (chs. 44–46), a life-giving river flowing from the temple that grows from ankle-deep to an uncrossable torrent and heals the Dead Sea (47:1–12), and a new allotment of the land around a city named 'The LORD Is There' (48:35).

Is this a blueprint for a literal future temple with sacrifices (a millennial temple), or a symbolic vision of restored worship fulfilled in Christ, the church and the new creation? The renewed sin and atonement offerings (43:19–27; 45:15–17) are the crux, in light of Hebrews 9–10.

A real temple to be built in Jerusalem for the millennial kingdom, from which Christ reigns. Older dispensationalists took the sacrifices as memorials of the cross, as the Lord's Supper is now; more recent writers (e.g. Hullinger) argue they provide ceremonial purification so that the holy presence of God can dwell among mortal, sinful people, without adding to Christ's atoning work.

The vision supplies exact measurements, named gates, priestly divisions and tribal boundaries; such detail, it is argued, makes little sense as mere symbol. Isaiah 56:6–7, 60:7 and Zechariah 14:16–21 also envisage worship and offerings among the nations in the age to come.

Critics note that 45:15–17 says the offerings 'make atonement', which seems to clash with Hebrews 10:18 ('no longer any offering for sin'). Proponents answer that the Levitical sacrifices never removed sin either (Hebrews 10:4) but dealt with ritual purity, and that the same will be true of millennial sacrifices.

An apocalyptic-symbolic vision of the restored presence of God, fulfilled in Christ, who is the true temple (John 2:19–21), in the church as God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21), and finally in the new Jerusalem, which has no temple because God and the Lamb are its temple (Revelation 21:22). The river of 47:1–12 reappears in Revelation 22:1–2 and in Jesus's promise of living water (John 7:37–39).

Revelation 21–22 deliberately reworks Ezekiel 40–48 (measuring, the high mountain, twelve gates, the river and trees whose leaves heal); the symmetrical dimensions and perfect square suggest an idealized vision; Hebrews forbids a return to the shadows.
Dispensationalists respond that symbolic readings cannot explain why so much non-symbolic detail is given, and that John's use of Ezekiel does not mean Ezekiel had nothing literal in view.

Shares the symbolic-fulfilment reading, but stresses the river of chapter 47 as a picture of the gospel's progressive growth in history: it deepens stage by stage until it fills the land and heals the Dead Sea, so the kingdom flowing from Christ's temple will gradually bring life to the nations before the end.

The ever-deepening river matches the growth parables of Matthew 13:31–33 and the stone becoming a mountain (Daniel 2:35); the healing of the nations (Revelation 22:2) is taken as a process now under way.

Amillennialists caution that Revelation 22 places the river in the consummated new creation, not in pre-consummation history; dispensationalists hold that the river is geographically real (Zechariah 14:8).

An idealized theological portrait of perfected worship that was never meant to be built: Ezekiel is shown what God's dwelling among a holy people must be, with access, holiness and life spreading outward. Some add that it held out a conditional pattern for the exiles (43:10–11), which they failed to implement, and that its permanent truth is realized in Christ and the new creation.

Ezekiel receives no command to build (contrast Exodus 25:9); the dimensions are schematic; the land allotment ignores real geography; Block reads chs. 40–48 as a theological 'constitution' for restored Israel rather than a construction plan.
Literal interpreters reply that 'never meant to be built' makes much of the detail pointless; others note that the conditional view raises the question why the returnees did not adopt it.

Historic premillennialists vary: many follow a typological reading fulfilled in Christ and the new creation, while some allow that elements may have a literal expression in Christ's millennial reign, though without the restoration of atoning sacrifices.
The historic-premillennial tradition does not rest its case on Old Testament temple prophecies but on Revelation 20, so it can read Ezekiel 40–48 with the typological tools of New Testament usage.

Dispensationalists see this as inconsistent: a literal millennium in Revelation 20 but a symbolic temple in Ezekiel. Amillennialists say a symbolic Ezekiel removes a main support for an earthly interregnum.
They Will Look on Me, the One They Have Pierced

In a section where the LORD defends Jerusalem against the nations (12:1–9), he promises to pour out on the house of David and Jerusalem a 'spirit of grace and supplication', so that they look on the one they pierced and mourn as for an only son, a mourning compared to that at Hadad-rimmon (12:11), followed by a fountain opened for cleansing from sin (13:1).

When and how does this mourning happen? John 19:37 applies the verse to the crucifixion and Revelation 1:7 to a coming with the clouds. Is it fulfilled at the cross and Pentecost, at AD 70, or in a future national repentance of Israel at the Second Coming?

A future national repentance of Israel at the close of the Tribulation: as the nations besiege Jerusalem (12:2–9; 14:1–3), the surviving Jewish people recognize Jesus as the Messiah they rejected, mourn, and are cleansed (13:1), and Christ returns to deliver them. Some teachers make this national confession the trigger for the Second Coming (compare Hosea 5:15; Matthew 23:39).

The setting is military and national (Jerusalem, the house of David, clan by clan, 12:12–14); it parallels Romans 11:26 ('all Israel will be saved') and Matthew 24:30, where the 'tribes' mourn when they see the Son of Man.

Critics point out that John 19:37 already treats the piercing as fulfilled at Calvary and that Acts 2:37–41 records Jerusalem's 'cut to the heart' repentance at Pentecost. Dispensationalists reply that the piercing was fulfilled at the cross while the national looking and mourning remain future.

The piercing is fulfilled at the crucifixion (John 19:37); the outpoured Spirit of grace and the repentance of Jerusalem's people begin at Pentecost (Acts 2:17, 37–38), and the fountain for cleansing is Christ's atoning work. Revelation 1:7 widens the circle to 'all the tribes of the earth', who will mourn at Christ's final, visible return.

The New Testament's two citations bracket the age: the cross (John 19:37) and the consummation (Revelation 1:7). Peter's Pentecost sermon matches the elements of 12:10 (outpoured Spirit, guilt for the crucified one, mourning, cleansing in baptism).
Dispensationalists object that Pentecost involved thousands, not the house of David 'clan by clan'; postmillennialists add that Romans 11 still anticipates a broader turning of Israel.

Fulfilled initially at the cross and Pentecost, and to be fulfilled more fully when the Spirit brings a widespread conversion of the Jewish people within history, as the Puritans expected from Romans 11; this conversion will be a great blessing to the world.
Romans 11:12, 15 promises greater riches for the world through Israel's 'fullness'; the Spirit-wrought repentance of 12:10 fits a revival, not a coercive event at the Parousia.
Amillennialists question whether Romans 11 teaches a future mass conversion; dispensationalists argue the passage's battle setting points to the end of history, not a gradual revival.

Revelation 1:7, which combines Daniel 7:13 with Zechariah 12:10, describes Christ's 'coming in clouds' of judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70: 'those who pierced him' are the first-century generation, and the 'tribes of the land' (Greek gē can mean land) are the clans of Judea mourning their judgment.

Revelation's time markers ('soon', 1:1; 'near', 1:3) and Jesus's warning to the high priest that he would 'see' the Son of Man coming (Matthew 26:64) fit a first-century audience; Zechariah 12:12–14 itself speaks of Israelite clans.

Critics note that in Zechariah 12 the mourning is repentance granted by grace and Jerusalem is defended, not destroyed, so AD 70 is an odd fulfilment; Thomas Ice presses this point. Preterists respond that Revelation 1:7 reapplies Zechariah's imagery, and that mourning can be lament under judgment as well as repentance.

Both the looking and the coming of Revelation 1:7 were completed in AD 70, when Christ came in the Father's glory and judged the generation that pierced him; there is no further visible coming to await.

Takes the time texts of Revelation and Matthew 26:64 as strictly limiting the fulfilment to the first-century generation, and notes that 'those who pierced him' (Revelation 1:7) names a specific first-century group who would see the coming.

This reading denies a future visible return, placing it outside the historic creeds (Nicene Creed, 'he will come again in glory'); critics also note Revelation 1:7 says 'every eye' will see him. Proponents answer that 'every eye' is idiomatic for those involved, as in Matthew 26:64.
Agrees that the piercing was fulfilled at Calvary but expects a future spiritual turning of Israel at or just before Christ's return, linked to Romans 11:26 and followed by Christ's earthly reign.
Holds together John 19:37, Revelation 1:7 and Romans 11 without requiring a pretribulational framework.
Amillennialists question the future mass-conversion premise; dispensationalists see the historic-premillennial treatment of Israel as underdeveloped.
The Day of the LORD on the Mount of Olives

All nations gather to battle against Jerusalem; the city is taken and half its people exiled (14:1–2). Then the LORD goes out to fight; his feet stand on the Mount of Olives, which splits east and west (14:3–5). A unique day follows, living waters flow from Jerusalem east and west, the LORD becomes king over all the earth, and Jerusalem dwells securely (14:6–11). Later verses (14:16–21) have survivors of the nations going up yearly to keep the Feast of Booths.

Is this a literal end-time battle and topographical change at Christ's return before an earthly millennium, a symbolic portrait of God's victory fulfilled in Christ and the church, or a picture partly fulfilled in the Roman siege of AD 70 and the gospel's spread from Jerusalem?

A future siege of Jerusalem at the end of the Tribulation (Armageddon), ended by Christ's bodily return to the Mount of Olives (compare Acts 1:11–12), a real earthquake reshaping the land, and the start of his millennial reign. Because the nations who refuse to keep the Feast of Booths are punished (14:16–19), sin and death still exist: this cannot be the eternal state, so it must be the millennium.

The geographic precision (Mount of Olives 'east of Jerusalem', specific gates and towers, 14:10), the link with Acts 1:11–12, and the presence of disobedience after the Lord becomes king all support an earthly interregnum.

Non-dispensationalists answer that prophetic idiom (compare Micah 1:3–4) often uses mountains splitting for theophany, and that the reinstated Feast of Booths with temple vessels and cooking pots (14:20–21) is the language of Israel's worship used for a reality the New Testament fulfils in Christ.

An apocalyptic picture of the decisive victory of God over the nations and the universal reign of the LORD, fulfilled in Christ's first coming, the outpouring of the Spirit (the 'living waters' of 14:8, compare John 7:37–39 and Ezekiel 47), the ingathering of the nations into the worship of God, and the final consummation where night ceases (14:7; Revelation 22:5).

Revelation picks up Zechariah 14's motifs (no night, light from God, living water, 'no longer any curse', 14:11; Revelation 22:3) for the new creation; the 'holy to the LORD' inscription spread to ordinary pots (14:20–21) signals the end of the sacred-common distinction realized in Christ.

Dispensationalists object that the 'symbolic' reading is selective, conceding the literal Mount of Olives in Acts 1 while denying it here; they also ask how the eternal state can contain nations that refuse to worship (14:17).

Verses 1–2 describe Rome's siege and capture of Jerusalem in AD 70, a 'day of the LORD' in which God used the nations to judge the city; the LORD's going out and the waters flowing from Jerusalem are the gospel's advance from Jerusalem to the nations (Acts 1:8), and the Lord's universal kingship is Christ's present reign.
Jesus's Olivet prophecy (spoken on the Mount of Olives) echoes the capture, the plundering and flight of 14:2–5 (Luke 21:20–24), and Acts 1–2 begins the outflow from Jerusalem.

Ice argues that Zechariah 14 shows the LORD rescuing Jerusalem and fighting against its attackers, the reverse of AD 70; preterists answer that 14:1–2 is judgment on the city and 14:3ff. the vindication of the faithful remnant and church, who fled and survived (Luke 21:21).

Emphasizes 14:9 ('the LORD will be king over all the earth') and 14:16–21 as a progressive historical triumph: through the gospel, the nations increasingly come to worship the true God, and the whole of life becomes 'holy to the LORD' before Christ's final return.
Coheres with Psalm 22:27–28, Isaiah 2:2–4 and the growth parables; the 'holiness' inscribed on bells and cooking pots pictures the sanctification of culture.
